short: His histories of the early empire remain the sharpest surviving account of imperial Rome.
full:
Publius Cornelius Tacitus, born around AD 56, rose through the Roman senatorial career under Vespasian, Titus and Domitian before turning to history writing under Trajan. His Annals and Histories cover the emperors from Tiberius to Domitian in prose famous for its compression, irony and suspicion of imperial power, shaped by his experience of Domitian's terror. His earlier Agricola and Germania are the fullest Roman accounts of Britain and the peoples beyond the Rhine.

Much of the Annals survives only in fragments, but what remains, including the passage describing Nero's persecution of Christians after the fire of AD 64, is the single most cited literary source for the first-century empire. Tacitus died around AD 120, and his unsparing portraits of tyranny and flattery shaped how later centuries read the entire principate.
